section_summary: This section assembles a newspaper warning about Japanese acquisition of Peruvian farmland, a lengthy U.S. Embassy assessment of Japanese immigration and economic penetration, and supporting commercial and consular reports. The documents examine Japanese influence in agriculture, retailing, manufacturing, shipping, and arms purchases, while evaluating allegations that Chimbote or other Pacific locations might become Japanese naval bases. Detailed trade and shipping tables document Japanese imports, Peruvian exports, passenger movements, and Nippon Yusen Kaisha cargoes; the final report turns to broader claims about the Galápagos Islands, the Panama Canal, and continental defense.

subfiles.title: Letter to the Director of La Crónica on Japanese Acquisition of Peruvian Farmland
subfiles.doc_type: newspaper letter/clipping enclosed with a consular report
subfiles.about: Lummis warns that Japanese tenants and agricultural workers are acquiring control of fertile coastal lands and urges legal restrictions protecting Peruvian cultivators and laborers.
subfiles.summary: The writer presents Japanese economic competition and the so-called peaceful invasion as a serious Peruvian social and agricultural problem. He alleges that Japanese farmers offer uneconomically high rents, concentrate on cotton, displace national workers, and contribute to shortages and higher prices for food crops. He proposes requiring landowners and tenants to reserve most tenancies and agricultural employment for Peruvians.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3634: Japanese Penetration in Peru
subfiles.from: Louis C. Dreyfus Jr., Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, U.S. Embassy, Lima
subfiles.about: The Embassy evaluates Carleton Beals's allegations about Japanese immigration, commercial and agricultural expansion, political influence, military contacts, arms purchases, and possible strategic interest in Peru.
subfiles.summary: Dreyfus considers much of Beals's report familiar or exaggerated but concludes that Japanese immigration and planned economic penetration have secured a substantial position in Peru. The despatch surveys immigration policy, Japanese community institutions and propaganda, anti-Japanese press and political agitation, agricultural landholding, commerce, industrial competition, and enforcement of Peru's eighty-percent employment laws. It also examines Peruvian arms purchases from Japan during the Leticia conflict, payments through guano shipments, and rumors concerning Asia Island and Chimbote. Although it finds no proof that Chimbote is becoming a Japanese naval base, it warns that Japanese influence could have strategic implications and encloses specialized commercial and consular reports.

subfiles.title: Partial List of Previous Embassy Despatches on the Japanese Situation in Peru
subfiles.about: This enclosure lists earlier embassy despatches concerning Japanese activities and influence in Peru.
subfiles.summary: The list identifies numbered despatches dating from 1926 through May 1934. It documents the substantial prior reporting record to which Despatch No. 3634 refers.

subfiles.title: Japanese Trade Activities in Peru
subfiles.about: Smith quantifies the rapid growth of Japanese imports and distribution networks in Peru and their effects on Peruvian, American, and European producers.
subfiles.summary: The report attributes Japanese trade gains to low prices, yen depreciation, organized export promotion, subsidized shipping, and an expanding network of Japanese wholesalers and retailers. Detailed statistics cover cotton textiles, knit goods, hosiery, cement, lamps, pharmaceuticals, toothpaste, and prospective iron and steel sales, showing particularly strong Japanese advances in inexpensive consumer goods. It also records growing Peruvian exports to Japan, including cotton, alpaca wool, coffee, and guano supplied outside ordinary customs statistics. Smith concludes that Japanese competition is strengthening demands for higher tariffs, immigration limits, and enforcement of Peru's eighty-percent employment legislation.

subfiles.title: Notes on Japanese Activities in Peru
subfiles.doc_type: confidential consular report with statistical appendices
subfiles.from: Arthur D. Jukes, American Vice Consul, Callao
subfiles.to: American Consul General James Barclay Young, for the U.S. Embassy, Lima
subfiles.about: Jukes investigates Japanese immigration, business, agriculture, shipping, and alleged strategic designs, especially claims that Chimbote could become a Japanese naval base.
subfiles.summary: The report finds the alleged Japanese takeover of Chimbote exaggerated: Japanese residents dominate much local petty commerce but have made limited agricultural inroads, while the harbor itself is exceptionally suitable for naval use. It describes Nippon Yusen Kaisha routes, passengers, freight, concealed wartime cargoes, and detailed Japanese-vessel cargo movements at Callao and other Peruvian ports from 1932 through 1934. Jukes also discusses unsuccessful or rumored Japanese efforts to acquire the Peruvian Steamship Company and reproduces an N.Y.K. circular establishing a Philippine–Gulf of Mexico–Caribbean service. The surviving section ends during a translated Peruvian naval memorandum advocating hemispheric cooperation to protect the Galápagos Islands, Panama Canal, and other strategic positions from a supposed Japanese threat.
